item.title: Can Long-Distance Hiking Support Trauma Recovery?
item.description:
Trauma

Can Long-Distance Hiking Support Trauma Recovery?

Walking on a trail may help transform pain for some trauma survivors

Posted June 4, 2026

Key points
  • Time on the hiking trail may offer meaningful therapeutic healing.
  • A long hike may help re-write the relationship someone has with suffering.
  • Sometimes, however, long-distance hiking can become a means of avoidance.
Source: Kampus Production via Pexels

For many long-distance hikers, the trail provides more than just a hike. Often, the trail represents a transformative opportunity, acting as a liminal space between who someone was and who they hope to become. And for those who have experienced trauma, time on the trail may offer meaningful therapeutic healing, at least in part, for some of the ways that traumatic experiences have shaped them. Extended time in the wilderness offers space to process life experiences that might not otherwise have time to be fully digested, while also helping to reshape internal narratives about the self in therapeutic landscapes.

Walking off the war

In 1948, World War II Veteran Earl Schaffer set out on the unmaintained Appalachian Trail in an attempt to “walk off the war." While the diagnostic label of post-traumatic stress disorder was not used at that time, Earl reported feeling “hopeless and broken-hearted” (Ross, 2021). He wrote about his experience on the rugged trail and processed the journey in a journal that he carried with him. He believed that the hike saved his life, re-igniting him with a sense of purpose and mending at least some of his ability to trust others again, through acts of kindness from strangers whom he called “trail angels” in small towns along the route (Ross, 2021). He is believed to have been the first to complete a thru-hike of the Appalachian Trail, and his journey laid a foundation for others looking to take a similar path: healing trauma, at least in part, through long-distance hiking.

The thru-hiking culture often associates the pursuit of long-distance trails with personal healing. Many hikers show up to the start of a long-distance hike following significant life thresholds like the death of a family member, a divorce, burnout, or addiction recovery. In Cheryl Strayed’s popular personal memoir, Wild, she faces a series of life events and sets out on the Pacific Crest Trail to process her grief and rebuild her self-trust and identity following significant upheavals.

A vicarious expression of emotional pain

Trauma often leaves people carrying invisible psychological pain that feels overwhelming. For some hikers, the trail becomes a place where this inner suffering can be translated into the language of the body; the physical suffering of the journey—sore muscles, exhaustion, and discomfort—can act as a tangible outlet for emotional suffering that may encounter barriers to being verbally expressed. Pilgrimage researcher Keith Egan observed that effort, fatigue, pain, and movement can become meaningful expressions of personal struggle. In this way, the trail can transform invisible wounds into something tangible. Hardship can become transformational because of the meaning behind it.

But can long-distance hiking heal trauma?

But can long-distance hiking actually help support trauma recovery? It may enhance trauma recovery, at least in part, by increasing self-efficacy, creating opportunities for meaning-making, and providing space to process. But recovery from trauma requires appropriate conditions and the ability to rebuild a sense of safety, trust, agency, and connection to oneself and others. Research shows that long-distance hiking helps reduce trauma symptoms for many participants. Warrior Expeditions, a veteran nonprofit outdoor therapy program, finds a clinically significant decrease in PTSD symptoms following combat veterans’ long-term wilderness experiences.

Source: Yevhen Sukhenko via Pexels

Rewriting the story of experiencing suffering

Jocelyn Smith, also known by her trail name Unhinged Hiker, is a thru-hiker recovering from complex trauma who believes that time on the trail offers an opportunity to rewrite internal narratives in relation to enduring challenges and suffering. “There are many long-distance hikers who have experienced childhood trauma. For some of us, the trail is more than an endurance sport; it becomes a way of reclaiming suffering itself. The challenge, exhaustion, and perseverance echo earlier hardships, but this time the struggle is chosen. This time, purpose and reward are waiting on the other side. In many ways, long-distance hiking can feel like rewriting the story of suffering—transforming pain from something that once happened to you into something you move through with strength, agency, and intention. Re-writing the story of experiencing suffering is profoundly empowering.”

Outdoor adventure research backs up this idea. When outdoor challenges and risks are chosen voluntarily, they can create opportunities for empowerment, self-efficacy, and the expansion of identity.

Often, trauma leaves people feeling powerless and in doubt of their own capabilities. The trail provides opportunities to solve problems and adapt to the ever-changing natural environment, increasing a sense of self-efficacy. These experiential learning opportunities help rebuild trust in oneself and foster a sense of personal agency and embodied competence.

Hiking can also become avoidance

Occasionally, extensive time on the trail becomes a way for people to avoid their problems rather than a space to process or integrate resolution into their lives. Constant movement may serve as an attempt to outpace the emotions beneath the surface of difficult life circumstances as movement feels more manageable than stillness. When hiking serves to avoid people or vulnerability in the long term, it may be maladaptive rather than integrative and beneficial.

It’s also worth noting that not everyone feels safe in the wilderness, and without a baseline of feeling safe, recovering from traumatic experiences can be difficult. The lived experiences that someone carries within them onto the trail, including aspects of their personal identity, will likely influence how they interpret the experience; what may feel therapeutic to one person may feel vulnerable or too far beyond the comfort zone of someone else.

Spending time in the wilderness on a long-distance hike may not eliminate all the psychological impacts of trauma, but it does offer opportunities for healing at least some of them.

item.title: Compassion Satisfaction: Finding Pleasure in Caring for Others
item.description:
Altruism

Compassion Satisfaction: Finding Pleasure in Caring for Others

How to heal the hurt that comes with caring.

Posted June 4, 2026

Key points
  • Caring isn’t the problem—lack of boundaries is.
  • When balanced, caring leads to greater well-being, resilience, and purpose.
  • Shift from “give until it hurts” to “give until it feels good.”
Source: kamon_saejueng/Adobe Free Stock

“When you perceive that an act done to another is done to yourself, you have understood the great truth.” — Lao Tzu

The Cost of Caring

Is caring for others a strength or a risk? It seems surprising that there are competing views on this question. From discussions of compassion fatigue to cautionary warnings about excessive empathy, the jury is still out on whether caring for others comes at a personal cost.

As a psychotherapist, I have routinely worked with individuals in caregiving roles, both professional and personal, as well as those with a strong, natural inclination to care for others. For many, this drive is simply part of who they are; considering others’ needs is a reflex rather than a choice.

It is widely understood that when we open our hearts and extend compassion, we risk being hurt. The saying “no good deed goes unpunished” reflects a common reality: Repeated disappointments can lead to burnout, frustration, and heartache. Over time, this may result in an overcorrection—shifting toward self-protection and even selfishness as a form of emotional armor.

Despite strong philosophical, spiritual, and psychological evidence that helping others ultimately benefits ourselves, there is a growing belief that overdoing it can increase stress and suffering. While we have moved beyond the self-focus of the 1970s “Me Generation,” the pendulum may now be swinging back. The advice to “put your oxygen mask on first” has expanded into a broader caution about giving too much in many areas of life.

What Is Compassion Satisfaction?

In response to the rise of compassion fatigue in the early 1990s, Dr. B. Hudnall Stamm introduced the concept of compassion satisfaction (CS) as a counterbalance to the emotional toll of caring.

Simply put, compassion satisfaction is the sense of fulfillment and meaning that comes from helping others. It does not require self-sacrifice; rather, it often emerges through everyday acts of kindness, such as:

  • Supporting a friend through a difficult time
  • Helping a family member manage stress
  • Volunteering in your community
  • Performing small acts of kindness for strangers

These acts often lead to meaningful emotional experiences, including:

  • A sense of warmth or emotional uplift
  • Greater connection and closeness with others
  • Feeling useful, kind, and aligned with your values
  • Quiet pride in doing the right thing
  • Increased meaning in daily life

Why Isn’t Helping Always Encouraged?

Given these positive outcomes, it may seem puzzling that helping others is not universally promoted as a key to well-being and happiness.

The caution lies in recognizing how thin the line can be between healthy giving and unhealthy overextension. In my work, and in the experiences of many caregivers, boundaries often determine the outcome. As the saying goes, “People will wipe their feet on anything with ‘welcome’ written on it.” Without limits, even well-intentioned generosity can be exploited.

Common Traps That Reduce Satisfaction

Certain patterns can diminish the positive effects of caring for others:

  • Feeling that your efforts go unnoticed
  • Taking on too much without adequate support
  • Holding yourself to unrealistic standards (“I should handle everything”)
  • Focusing only on problems rather than positive outcomes

The Benefits of Compassion Satisfaction

Beyond simply “feeling good,” compassion satisfaction offers tangible psychological and emotional benefits:

  • Improved overall well-being and mood
  • Stronger, more meaningful relationships
  • Increased resilience during personal stress
  • Reduced emotional exhaustion in caregiving roles (e.g., parenting, supporting friends)
  • A deeper sense of purpose in everyday life

What Compassion Satisfaction Is Not...

  • Always saying “yes” to requests for help.
  • Ignoring one’s own needs.
  • Solving other people’s problems.
  • Always being available.
  • Rescuing others.
  • Doing everything right.

A Healthier Way to Give

Compassion satisfaction is becoming an essential protective factor, particularly for those in helping professions where burnout is increasingly common. However, it is equally valuable for anyone who cares for others in their personal life.

We’ve all heard: “Give until it hurts.” Compassion satisfaction offers a better approach: “Give until it feels good." Caring for others doesn’t have to come at your expense. With the right boundaries, it can be one of the most reliable ways to sustain your own well-being while making a meaningful difference in someone else’s life.

item.title: Are You Attracted to a Person or a Pattern?
item.description:
Relationships

Are You Attracted to a Person or a Pattern?

The surprising reasons we keep falling for the same people.

Posted June 4, 2026

Key points
  • People may choose partners who are more similar than chance would predict.
  • Having a "type" may be less about people and more about recurring relationship patterns.
  • Understanding recurring relationship patterns can help us make more intentional choices.

Do we all have a "type"? Most people believe they do.

Ask someone about their dating history, and they'll often notice a pattern. Maybe they've repeatedly fallen for artists, athletes, intellectuals, bad boys, emotionally unavailable partners, or people who need rescuing. Sometimes the similarities are obvious. Other times, they are harder to spot. The faces, careers, and personalities may differ, but the emotional dynamic feels strangely familiar.

This raises a question: Do we really have a “type,” or do we simply keep repeating relationship patterns?

Research suggests the answer may be both.

On one hand, people do show relatively stable preferences when it comes to romantic attraction. Studies have found that people tend to pair with others who share similarities in education, values, personality traits, and even physical characteristics.

But that's only part of what's happening.

Psychologists have long observed that people often recreate familiar relationship dynamics, even when those dynamics are painful. The phenomenon is sometimes explained through attachment theory. Our earliest relationships help shape expectations about closeness, trust, conflict, and emotional availability. These expectations can become templates that influence whom we find attractive later in life.

So, a person's “type” may not be a particular look or personality. It may be a familiar emotional experience.

For example, someone who grew up working hard for approval may find themselves repeatedly drawn to partners who are difficult to please. Another person may consistently pursue emotionally distant partners, mistaking the pursuit of connection for chemistry.

Maybe that’s why some people seem to date the same person over and over again in different bodies.

The pattern is rarely conscious. Few people wake up and decide to seek out relationships that will frustrate them. Yet familiarity has a powerful pull. Research suggests that humans generally prefer what is familiar, even when that familiarity is imperfect. The known often feels safer than the unknown. But just because something feels familiar doesn't mean it's good for us.

So, here’s the problem: The relationships that feel most exciting or magnetic are not always the ones best suited for long-term happiness. Sometimes, intense attraction reflects genuine compatibility. Other times, it reflects the activation of old emotional patterns.

So, do we all have a type?

Perhaps a better question is this: Are we attracted to particular types of people, or are we attracted to particular kinds of emotional experiences? The answer might explain why some of us keep ending up in relationships that look different on the surface but feel surprisingly similar.

But attraction patterns are not destiny.

People can develop greater awareness of the dynamics that repeatedly appear in their relationships. That's why it can be useful to pay attention not just to who attracts us, but to the patterns underneath that attraction.

Sometimes what feels like chemistry is really familiarity. And sometimes the healthiest relationships don't feel familiar at all, at least not at first.

item.title: Types of Psychological Testing
item.description:
Psychological Evaluation

Types of Psychological Testing

There are many subtypes of valid psychological testing suitable for guiding diagnosis.

Posted June 4, 2026

Source: OlgaNeuroArt/Adobe Stock

Psychologists are often asked to complete assessments, or testing. As a clinical psychologist with primary training focus in pediatric neuropsychology, I frequently get asked to complete neuropsychological assessments, and this term has a very specific meaning. For those in the neuropsychology world, this assessment would be for a child with a known history of a brain injury or illness that likely impacts one’s neurological functioning, such as a brain tumor, seizures, or a serious concussion.

However, when I speak to the parents or referring professionals, the request is usually for the assessment of IQ or learning disorders; an assessment psychologist would call this request academic achievement and not neuropsychology. These experiences lead me to believe that a brief explanation of the different types of psychological assessment might be beneficial.

What is psychological testing or assessment?

Psychological assessment refers to the process psychologists use to evaluate an individual’s cognitive, emotional, behavioral, and personality functioning. This process often includes clinical interviews, behavioral observations, record reviews, and the administration of standardized psychological measures. Standardized measures are carefully developed tests that are administered and scored in a consistent manner, allowing an individual’s performance to be compared to that of others who are demographically similar (such as age, education, sex). An essential aspect of psychological assessment is the use of instruments with demonstrated reliability and validity. Reliability refers to the consistency and stability of test results over time and across settings, while validity refers to the degree to which a test accurately measures the construct (i.e. anxiety) it is intended to assess. Together, reliability and validity help ensure that assessment findings are accurate, meaningful, and appropriate for clinical, educational, or research decision-making.

Subtypes of Psychological Assessment

Subtypes of psychological testing have some degree of overlap because measures used in one type of assessment are often used in others. Also, some assessments may include several different types of testing in an effort to answer or address broader clinical questions.

Neuropsychological assessment is an assessment with a focus on cognitive functioning. Some areas commonly assessed include executive functioning, memory, fine and gross motor dexterity, processing speed, spatial awareness, and attention in addition to several other cognitive areas that may have been impacted by a neurological injury (i.e. traumatic brain injury, brain surgery) or neurological disorder (i.e. Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s). Results of testing may assist in the detection of a progressive neurological disorder, treatment planning, including the development of compensatory strategies, as well as environment and behavioral changes that may benefit the individual and their family or caretakers. For school-aged individuals, the results of testing can aid in the development of academic accommodations, and strategies for use within the school setting and/or for standardized tests (i.e. SAT, LSAT, GMAT).

Academic achievement testing has many similarities to neuropsychological assessment in that both are cognitively based, and both often include IQ testing. However, unlike neuropsychology, achievement testing is less concerned with how one’s brain works and is more focused on what one has learned and one’s ability to apply their cognitive abilities to areas of learning (i.e. sight reading, phonics, mathematical concepts). Academic achievement assessment is aimed at identifying or ruling out the presence of learning disabilities that may impact one’s ability to perform at maximum potential academically or on standardized tests. Results of testing can aid in the development of academic accommodation and strategies for use within the school setting and/or for standardized tests (i.e. ACT, GRE, MCAT).

Developmental psychological assessments have their own similarities with achievement and neuropsychological assessments in that they, too, usually have a cognitive component. The goal of developmental assessments is to identify or rule out the presence of neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism. Other referral reasons for this type of assessment include intellectual disability, language disorders, and coordination disorders. Of all the assessment types, this assessment starts at the youngest age range, with toddlers often being appropriate for these assessments.

The most common neurodevelopmental disorder is attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). ADHD-specific assessments may, again, include IQ testing and specific cognitive areas that are often impacted by ADHD, such as planning and organization. Other mental health disorders may also be assessed to rule out other conditions that may mimic or exacerbate ADHD, such as anxiety, trauma, or substance use. These assessments can aid in the development of academic accommodations and strategies for use within the school setting and/or for standardized tests and assist prescribing clinicians in pharmacological treatment planning.

Personality assessment is the one most people think about when they hear “psychological testing,” the type portrayed in movies with inkblots, and the type that leads to the casual question of “what personality type are you?” This assessment type is used most for general diagnostic clarity. Not only is this type of assessment used to determine diagnoses, but it also gives the provider and individual useful information on how they see, react to, and cope with everyday life and the challenges that come with it and how the personality traits influence one’s mental health and general functioning.

Ultimately, the assessment you receive would ideally be based on the question or problem you are looking to understand better.

Alton Bozeman, PsyD, is the Director of The Menninger Assessment Center. He is noted for his expertise in neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism, ADHD, and intellectual disability.

item.title: Why Psychological Safety Matters More in AI-Enabled Teams
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Why Psychological Safety Matters More in AI-Enabled Teams

4 steps to increase trust on your work teams.

Posted June 4, 2026

Key points
  • Psychological safety is crucial for successful AI integration in workplace teams.
  • Junior and female employees report feeling least psychologically safe in teams.
  • AI introduces new team trust issues, as AI mistakes can't be challenged like human errors.

The conversation about AI at work has become dominated by speed, efficiency, and productivity gains. Leaders are under pressure to move quickly, experiment publicly, and integrate AI into everyday workflows before they fall behind. But in the rush to adopt new technology, many organizations are overlooking one of the most important, foundational conditions for successful AI integration: psychological safety. In AI-enabled teams, employees must feel safe enough to ask questions, challenge outputs, admit uncertainty, experiment without fear of embarrassment, and speak up when something feels ethically, strategically, or operationally wrong. Without that foundation of trust, even the most sophisticated AI strategy will stall—not because the technology failed, but because people stopped engaging honestly with it.

AI, Psychological Safety, and Junior Talent Development

Psychological safety is the belief that you can be yourself, take good risks, ask questions, share partially formed ideas, raise problems, and respectfully disagree within your work teams without the worry of being embarrassed, singled out, or penalized. When employees feel psychologically safe, they feel comfortable speaking up and are far more likely to identify serious errors or problems earlier. They are also more likely to think creatively, share innovative ideas, and share their expertise, all of which matter in the context of work generally and AI integration specifically.

I recently had the opportunity to measure psychological safety in the legal profession. Approximately half of the nearly 900 survey respondents felt like their work efforts were not deliberately undermined, their unique skills and talents were valued at work, and they were able to bring up problems and tough issues at work. However, more than 40 percent of respondents found it difficult to ask for help, almost one-third reported that mistakes were often held against them, and nearly 20 percent said they felt rejected for being different.

The “psychologically unsafe” group responded “yes” to these statements:

  • It is difficult to ask others for help.
  • If I make a mistake, it is often held against me.
  • I am sometimes rejected for being different.

This “psychologically unsafe” group was almost 70 percent female and associates, and more than one-third were between 25 and 34 years old. Interestingly, a similar finding emerged in a study about burnout and psychological safety in medical school. That study found that female medical students perceived medical school as less psychologically safe than their male counterparts.

The psychologically unsafe group in law reported a lack of support for personal well-being/work-life balance, lack of sponsorship/mentorship, and dysfunctional firm culture more regularly compared to the general group in the additional question section of the survey.

Junior talent development is quickly becoming one of the hottest issues in law firms, across professional services, and in the workplace generally. How is junior talent supposed to gain judgment, learn through repetition, experiment with AI and changing workflows, and build new capabilities if a solid foundation of psychological safety isn’t present?

AI Integration and Teaming Challenges

AI integration doesn’t just surface technology issues—it also uncovers team dynamics issues. As organizations rapidly integrate AI at work, leaders are uncovering the impact of AI tools on team dynamics; specifically, team performance appears to be declining.

One of the reasons why teaming challenges arise is trust, because AI can change the dynamic within a team and introduce trust ambiguity. When the humans on teams make a mistake, other humans can ask questions to understand what happened, give context, and then figure out ways to prevent the mistake from happening again. This process of mutual learning, which strengthens teams, isn’t there with AI tools. Humans can’t challenge AI in the same way, which makes it hard for team members to understand what caused the error or how to prevent it from happening again.

AI doesn’t pick up on team contextual cues, adjust its communication style to match people on the team, or engage in informal relationship building with other team members. As a result, there can be a cost to team dynamics when an AI team member operates according to fundamentally different team rules.

4 Steps to Increase Psychological Safety on Your Work Teams

One way to help is to apply psychological safety principles to AI integration. Amy Edmondson and her colleagues recommend these steps:

  1. Reframe AI as a learning process, not just an execution process. This means that it’s important to position AI deployment as ongoing experimentation with hands-on learning.
  2. Model fallibility and curiosity. One of the biggest ways leaders create psychological safety is by acknowledging their own mistakes. Leaders can share their own mistakes with AI and what they learned.
  3. Create intelligent failure protocols. There are different types of failures. Did your team experience an “intelligent failure” or a “basic failure”? Intelligent failures happen when you’re testing new AI tools in new ways where the risks are low and mistakes should be celebrated as learning opportunities. Conversely, basic failures are mistakes that occur where limitations are already known and a basic process was missed.
  4. Emphasize human connection. As AI handles more routine tasks, what’s left is the more complex and interdependent work for teams. Leaders need to create space to discuss AI integration challenges. Leaders also need to be mindful of the importance of continued human-to-human interaction. One study found that 90 percent of workers see AI as a co-worker, 67 percent trust AI more than their colleagues, 64 percent say they have a better relationship with AI than with their human teammates, and 54 percent say AI is more empathetic. Team members need to also foster those same skills (trust, empathy, strong relationships) with each other.

As organizations race to build AI capability, the companies that will thrive are not necessarily the ones with the most advanced tools. They are the ones that create environments where people feel safe enough to learn, adapt, question, and collaborate alongside those tools. Psychological safety is not a “soft skill” or cultural nice-to-have. In an AI-enabled workplace, it is the infrastructure that allows innovation, trust, and human judgment to scale together.

item.title: Slowing Down and Listening to Your Inner Voice
item.description:
Self-Help

Slowing Down and Listening to Your Inner Voice

Give yourself permission to pause, pay attention, and choose differently.

Posted June 4, 2026

Key points
  • Self-care isn’t meant to be just another item on your to-do list.
  • Slowing down gives you space to notice, question, and gently challenge old narratives.
  • Listening inward takes courage, intention, and the willingness to set boundaries.

Somewhere along the way, many of us picked up stories about what it means to care for ourselves. Some of those stories taught us that rest is laziness, that slowing down is unproductive, or that self-care is selfish. Over time, these beliefs can become so deeply ingrained that even when our mind and body are asking for rest, it can still feel difficult to justify.

Our upbringing, cultural expectations, family dynamics, and professional environments can all reinforce these messages, making true rest feel uncomfortable, undeserved, or even shameful. There can be this feeling of guilt that accompanies it. And when do we feel guilty? We tend to feel guilty when we believe we’ve broken a rule. Sometimes these rules sound like: You can take care of yourself, but only after everything else is done. Rest has to be earned. Strong people keep going. Slowing down means you’re falling behind.

The challenge is that living in a constant state of pushing, producing, and trying to prove ourselves is often not sustainable, even if it’s normalized. Over time, it can come at the expense of our mental, emotional, and physical well-being.

The truth is, as adults, our work is rarely ever fully done. There will almost always be another email to answer, responsibility to carry, or task waiting for our attention. If we waited until every task was completed, we’d never make time for ourselves at all.

I recently had a conversation with clinical psychologist Natasha Ramzan about cultural narratives, self-care, and the pressure many people feel to keep pushing through. As she shared with me, just because it’s familiar doesn’t mean that it’s always healthy (Life by Design, 2026). She spoke about how it’s OK to want something different for yourself.

Part of healing and growth often involves unlearning the unsustainable expectations and norms we’ve inherited. It’s recognizing that self-care is not selfish; it’s an important part of how we care for our well-being and navigate life’s demands. When we tend to our own needs, we become more resourced, more present, and better able to show up for the people and responsibilities that matter to us.

The Power of Pausing

Many of us move through our days in constant motion, filling every space with “must-dos” and tasks that feel urgent. When we allow ourselves to slow down, even briefly, we interrupt the autopilot. We create space to notice the stories and impulses driving our behaviours, like the reflex to correct your child for watching TV on a sunny day, opening your laptop in the evening because relaxing feels less productive than getting ahead, or the urge to keep moving because slowing down might bring difficult thoughts or feelings to the surface.

It’s often in these moments that we begin to recognize how deeply old lessons from family, culture, or society have shaped our understanding of what is allowed, valued, or acceptable. Slowing down gives us the opportunity to gently ask ourselves: Is this true for me right now? What story am I telling myself? Am I operating from habit, or am I honouring the kind of life I want to build? What do I need right now?

Listening for Your Inner Voice

The pace and pressure of daily life can create so much noise that it becomes difficult to stay connected to our inner voice. Often, it’s only when we slow down that we can truly begin listening. Sometimes that inner voice is a gentle nudge: “You need rest. You’re allowed to choose ease. There is no prize for burnout.” Other times, we may notice a more critical voice emerge, one shaped by pressure, fear, perfectionism, or old expectations telling us we should be doing more, pushing harder, or proving ourselves. Part of the work is learning to recognize the difference between the inner critic and the inner coach, and to notice that shame or guilt can sometimes arise not because we’ve done something wrong, but because we’re beginning to challenge a belief about what we’re supposed to do or who we’re supposed to be.

People often ask me how to know which inner voice is truly theirs. In my book Stress Wisely, I write about how the voice that is kind, loving, compassionate, and steady is the real you. Trust that voice. It’s within that inner knowing that your wisest self speaks. When you meet yourself there, wellness begins to flow more naturally.

Awareness is the first step toward change. When we notice the old lessons we’ve picked up about rest, worth, and productivity, we create the opportunity to loosen their grip. Noticing when self-criticism or guilt shows up allows us to gently question it and let go of what’s no longer serving us.

One Thing for Your Head, Heart, and Body

Redefining self-care may mean unlearning and deconstructing the rulebook we were handed. It means recognizing that resting, slowing down, or carving out time for yourself is not lazy or selfish; it’s part of the work. It’s self-stewardship. At the same time, it’s important to remember that genuine self-care doesn’t look the same for everyone, and the goal is not for it to become yet another set of boxes to check off. The best self-care practices are the ones that feel good for you. What practices can you turn to, even on your hardest days?

My gentle invitation is to focus each day on doing one small act of self-stewardship for your head, heart, and body.

Head: Do something that brings mental clarity or calm. This might be tidying your space, making a to-do list, taking a moment of solitude, or even listening to a song that helps you process emotions.

Heart: Nurture your emotional well-being through connection, joy, or meaning. It could be reaching out to someone you love, reflecting on a cherished memory, laughing with a friend, or engaging in a practice that brings comfort.

Body: Support your body with movement, nourishment, rest, or gentleness. Maybe it’s a walk outside, a few minutes of breathwork, or simply giving yourself permission to slow down and honour what your body needs today.

Final Thoughts

Our worth remains intact no matter how much, or how little, we accomplish on any given day. When we choose to move differently than what has been modeled for us, or differently than what society or "hustle culture" says we should be doing, ought to be doing, or could be doing, it can feel uncomfortable.

It can take repeated intentionality to untangle self-worth from productivity and to practice self-kindness instead of self-criticism. Self-compassion and recognizing that it’s OK to want something different for yourself are often the starting points for unlearning these patterns and creating healthier ways of living and working.

Slowing down and listening inward allows us to align our days and our lives more closely with what truly matters. Give yourself permission to rest without guilt, to set boundaries with kindness, and to move at the pace your heart, mind, and body need.
